subject: Physics
title: Simple Machines Lab
summary: Levers, pulleys, a wheel and axle and an inclined plane: change the fulcrum, the ropes, the wheel or the ramp, read the force meter, and find out what you gain and what you pay for it. Predict first, then watch what really happens.

scenarios.title: The Lever Bench
scenarios.setup: A bar, a movable fulcrum and a load, with a force meter on the effort end. Slide the fulcrum and read the force. Real levers (a crowbar, a wheelbarrow, tweezers and more) are then set up on the bench one at a time.

law.name: Law of the lever
law.formula: effort × effort arm = load × load arm

trials.prompt: A 2 m bar lifts a 200 N load at one end, with you pushing down on the other end. The fulcrum is 1 m from the load and the force meter reads 200 N. You slide the fulcrum closer to the load, to 0.5 m. How much effort is needed now?
trials.outcome: 66.7 N: less than the 200 N.
trials.explanation: Effort × effort arm = load × load arm. Moving the fulcrum towards the load makes the load arm shorter and the effort arm longer, so the effort needed falls: 200 × 0.5 ÷ 1.5 = 66.7 N.

trials.prompt: The same 300 N load is lifted with a wheelbarrow (a class 2 lever) and with a pair of tweezers (a class 3 lever). Which needs less effort?
trials.outcome: The wheelbarrow: about 107 N, against 514 N.
trials.explanation: The effort depends on the effort arm and the load arm, not on how big the tool looks. The wheelbarrow needs 300 × 0.5 ÷ 1.4 = 107 N and the pair of tweezers needs 300 × 0.12 ÷ 0.07 = 514 N. A lever with the load between the fulcrum and the effort (class 2) has an effort arm longer than its load arm; one with the effort between the fulcrum and the load (class 3) has a shorter effort arm, so it needs more force.

effort arm: distance from the fulcrum to the effort

trials.prompt: A crowbar rests on a stone with its short end under a crate. You push down on the far end of the crowbar. The stone is between the crate and your hand. Which class of lever is this?
trials.outcome: Class 1: the fulcrum is in the middle.
trials.explanation: A class 1 lever has the fulcrum between the load and the effort, like a seesaw or a crowbar: the effort can be smaller or larger than the load, depending on which arm is longer.

scenarios.title: The Pulley Bench
scenarios.setup: One pulley fixed at the top of a frame, with a rope passing over it: the load hangs on one end and you pull the other end through a force meter. A ruler beside the frame measures how far the load rises and how much rope you pull. The last questions ask about movable pulleys and the block and tackle.

law.name: The fixed pulley
law.formula: effort = load; rope pulled = height lifted

trials.prompt: A 200 N load hangs on one end of the rope over the fixed pulley. You pull the other end down to lift it. Compared with the load's weight, what will the force meter read?
trials.outcome: About 200 N: the same as the load.
trials.explanation: The rope carries the same tension all the way along, and only one rope section holds the load up. So the pull you give equals the weight of the load: a single fixed pulley gives no saving in force.

variants.prompt: A 200 N load hangs on one end of the rope over the fixed pulley. You pull the other end down to lift it. Compared with the load's weight, what will the force meter read?
variants.outcome: About 200 N: the same as the load.
variants.explanation: The rope carries the same tension all the way along, and only one rope section holds the load up. So the pull you give equals the weight of the load: a single fixed pulley gives no saving in force.

variants.prompt: You pull the free end of the rope DOWN by 1.2 m. What does the 150 N load do?
variants.outcome: It rises by 1.2 m.
variants.explanation: The rope runs over the wheel, so pulling one side down pulls the other side up. A fixed pulley changes the direction of your force: you pull down and the load goes up.

variants.prompt: With the fixed pulley you pull 1.5 m of rope through your hands. How far does the 240 N load rise?
variants.outcome: 1.5 m: exactly as far as you pull.
variants.explanation: There is one rope section holding the load, so every metre you pull lifts the load one metre. No force is saved, so no distance is lost.

variants.prompt: A single fixed pulley does not reduce the force needed. Why do builders still use one to raise loads?

options.label: You can pull down instead of lifting up, and use your own weight
It adds energy to the load

variants.outcome: It lets you pull down, which is easier and lets you use your body weight.
variants.explanation: The force is the same, but its direction is changed. Pulling down is more comfortable than lifting, you can stand on the ground away from the load, and you can lean your weight into the rope.

variants.prompt: The 120 N load is lifted 2 m by pulling the rope over the fixed pulley. Compared with lifting it by hand, how much work did you do?
variants.outcome: The same: 240 J either way.
variants.explanation: Work = force × distance. With an ideal fixed pulley the force and the distance are both the same as lifting by hand, so the work is the same.

trials.prompt: First you lift the 200 N load straight up by hand, then you lift it the same height by pulling down on the rope over the fixed pulley. Which needs less force?
trials.outcome: Both need about 200 N: the fixed pulley saves no force at all.

law.name: Movable pulleys
law.formula: effort = load ÷ number of supporting ropes

trials.prompt: Now imagine a different set-up: the pulley hangs on the load itself (a movable pulley), with one end of the rope tied to the ceiling and you pulling the other end up. For a 200 N load, what is the effort?
trials.outcome: About 100 N: half the load.
trials.explanation: With a movable pulley, two rope sections hold the load up and share it equally, so each carries half and your pull is half the load.

variants.prompt: Now imagine a different set-up: the pulley hangs on the load itself (a movable pulley), with one end of the rope tied to the ceiling and you pulling the other end up. For a 200 N load, what is the effort?

variants.explanation: With a movable pulley, two rope sections hold the load up and share it equally, so each carries half and your pull is half the load.

variants.prompt: With a movable pulley, how much rope must you pull to raise a 160 N load by 1 m?
variants.outcome: 2 m: twice the height, because each of the two supporting ropes must shorten by 1 m.
variants.explanation: Halving the force doubles the distance: effort × distance stays the same.

law.name: Work is conserved
law.formula: effort × distance = load × distance

trials.prompt: A block and tackle holds a 320 N load on 4 rope sections. Compared with a single movable pulley (2 sections), what happens to the effort?
trials.outcome: 80 N: less than the 160 N of one movable pulley.
trials.explanation: With 4 supporting ropes the effort is 320 ÷ 4 = 80 N. But raising the load by 1 m means pulling 4 × 1 = 4 m of rope: the force is gained at the cost of distance.

variants.prompt: A block and tackle holds a 320 N load on 4 rope sections. Compared with a single movable pulley (2 sections), what happens to the effort?

variants.explanation: Every one of the 3 supporting ropes must shorten by 1 m, so you pull 3 m. Effort falls to 80 N, but the distance rises 3 times: effort × distance stays the same.

trials.prompt: A crane's hook block uses many pulleys. What is the benefit?

law.name: Wheel and axle

trials.prompt: A bucket of water weighs 120 N. It hangs on a rope wound round an axle of radius 5 cm. You turn a wheel of radius 20 cm fixed to the axle. Compared with lifting the bucket straight up by hand, how much force do you need at the rim of the wheel?

law.name: Inclined plane
law.formula: effort = load × height ÷ ramp length

trials.prompt: A 600 N crate must reach a truck bed 1.2 m high. You can lift it straight up, or push it up a smooth ramp 4.8 m long. Which needs less effort?

trials.explanation: Lifting straight up takes a force of 600 N over 1.2 m. The ramp needs only W × h ÷ length = 600 × 1.2 ÷ 4.8 = 150 N, but over 4.8 m. The same work is done with a smaller force over a longer distance.
